q-117666:
By the additive property of the definite integral, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-5}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-5}^{-1}(7-3x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{-1}^{1}10\,\text{d}x \\  & =(7x-3\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}){|}_{-5}^{-1}+10x{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =[7(-1)-3\frac{(-1)^{2}}{2}-7(-5)+3\frac{(-5)^{2}}{2}]+10[(1)-(-1)] \\  & =[28+36]+10[2] \\  & =64+20 \\  & =84.\end{aligned}
$$

q-106411:
The diagram shows that the parabola is vertical, has its vertex at $(0,0),$ and passes through the point $(6,9).$

The parametric equations of a vertical parabola  that has its vertex at $(0,0)$ are

$$
x=2pt,\,y=p{t}^{2},
$$

where $p$ is constant.

Since the parabola passes through $(6,9),$ we can substitute $x=6$ and $y=9$ into the standard parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}6=2pt \\ 9=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}6 & =2pt \\ 3 & =pt \\ t & =\frac{3}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}9 & =p{(\frac{3}{p})}^{2} \\ 9 & =p\cdot \frac{9}{{p}^{2}} \\ 9 & =\frac{9}{p} \\ p & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x=2(1)t,\,y=(1){t}^{2},
$$

which simplify to

$$
x=2t,\,y={t}^{2}.
$$

q-71882:
Let $\delta >0.$ A *neighborhood* of a point ${x}_{0}$ is the set of points whose distance from ${x}_{0}$ is less than $\delta .$

$$
\{x:|x-{x}_{0}|<\delta \}
$$

In two-dimensional space, a neighborhood of ${x}_{0}$ is the open disc $|x-{x}_{0}|<\delta ,$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097432/assets/50a6c72e169f3104eb0b9958673cc6644f770e6bcc3ebf23360eb20189325a28.png)

Furthermore, we have the following definitions:

- A point ${x}_{0}$ is an *interior point* of a set $S$ if $S$ contains *some* neighborhood of ${x}_{0}.$ The set of all interior points of $S$ is called the *interior* of $S.$

- A point ${x}_{0}$ is a *boundary point* of a set $S$ if *every* neighborhood of ${x}_{0}$ contains points that are in $S$ and points that are not in $S.$ 
The set of all boundary points of $S$ is called the *boundary* of $S.$

With that in mind, let's examine the statements in turn.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097432/assets/46670ef62c2afa2e5aa5c0eb4d1684493f35ab4f9a82aa5375994bf1cb2cb154.png)

$$

$$

- Statement I is true. Indeed, $A$ is a boundary point because every open neighborhood of $A$ contains points that belong to $M$ and points that do not belong to $M.$

- Statement II is false. The point $B$ is an interior point since there exists an open neighborhood of $B$ that is fully contained inside the set $M.$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, $C$ is an interior point since there exists an open neighborhood of $C$ that is fully contained inside the set $M.$

Therefore, the correct answer is 'I and III only'.
